one_liner: Three-way boundary error decomposition: how much reported boundary error is model, annotation, or metric artifact?
problem: Boundary metrics lump together model mislocalization, annotation imprecision, and rasterization/metric artifacts; the field optimizes the sum without knowing its composition.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: on standard benchmarks, at least half of measured boundary error within 3px of GT is attributable to annotation imprecision and rasterization (estimable via multi-annotation and re-rasterization controls), meaning models are closer to the achievable boundary ceiling than metrics suggest and sub-3px 'progress' claims are mostly noise-fitting.
why_important: Recalibrates what boundary improvements are real, and defines the achievable frontier every method should be compared against.
why_possibly_novel: A formal decomposition protocol with published per-benchmark error budgets is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Multi-annotate 200 object boundaries at high zoom, estimate annotation noise spectra, propagate through metrics, compare against published method deltas.
main_risk: Extrapolating from 200 objects to benchmark-wide claims needs careful sampling design.

one_liner: Size-stratified reporting flips leaderboards: mIoU improvements of recent methods concentrate entirely in large objects.
problem: mIoU weights pixels, so large objects dominate; two methods with equal mIoU can differ enormously on small objects, and progress claims may hide small-object stagnation.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: re-scoring the last 5 years of leading semantic/panoptic methods with size-stratified metrics shows near-zero progress in the smallest object decile (progress has been large-object progress), and ranking inversions occur for a substantial fraction of published comparisons.
why_important: If small-object performance has been flat while headlines improved, the field has been optimizing a metric artifact - a meta-finding that redirects evaluation practice.
why_possibly_novel: Longitudinal size-stratified meta-analysis of published models is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Download 10 public checkpoints spanning 5 years, evaluate size-stratified on ADE20K/Cityscapes, plot per-decile progress curves.
main_risk: Checkpoint availability and preprocessing comparability; must reproduce official numbers first.

one_liner: The upsampling ceiling: bilinear decoder interpolation imposes a hard boundary-sharpness floor that no training can cross.
problem: Virtually all decoders upsample coarse features with smooth interpolation; this architecturally bounds achievable boundary sharpness, but the bound has never been computed and compared with observed errors.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: for each common decoder design, there is a computable minimum boundary transition width (from the interpolation kernel and feature stride), observed model boundaries sit AT this floor (not above it), and boundary-error differences between published methods largely reduce to their upsampling-path differences - training and losses are second-order for sharpness.
why_important: Would reduce a confusing literature of boundary methods to an analyzable signal-processing property, telling designers exactly where sharpness comes from.
why_possibly_novel: Analytic sharpness-floor computation validated against model zoo behavior is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Derive floors for 5 decoder designs, measure boundary transition widths of corresponding checkpoints on step-edge probes, test floor-attainment.
main_risk: Learned upsampling components complicate the analysis; treat them as measurable empirical kernels.

one_liner: Thin structures break at regular intervals set by feature stride: connectivity failure is periodic, not random.
problem: Segmented wires, branches, and vessels show gaps. If gaps are periodic (aligned with stride/receptive-field geometry) rather than random, the failure is architectural aliasing with a specific signature and fix path.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: the autocorrelation of gap positions along thin structures shows peaks at multiples of the effective feature stride across architectures, and gap probability depends on the structure's sub-stride phase - connectivity failure is deterministic aliasing, falsifiable by phase-shifted re-inference reducing gaps.
why_important: Periodic failure implies cheap test-time fixes (phase ensembling) and indicts stride design rather than data or capacity for a classical failure mode.
why_possibly_novel: Gap-periodicity forensics on thin-structure segmentation is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Segment synthetic and real thin structures, compute gap-position autocorrelation vs stride, test phase-jitter ensembling.
main_risk: Multiple strides in pyramidal models blur the periodicity; analyze per-scale contributions.

one_liner: Which boundary errors do humans actually notice? Build the perceptual boundary metric from discrimination experiments.
problem: Boundary metrics (BF-score, boundary IoU) weight all deviations equally, but human observers notice some errors (corner cutting, protrusion loss) far more than others (smooth in/out breathing) - the perceptual weighting is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: human detection thresholds for boundary deviations vary by an order of magnitude across error types (systematic offsets vs high-frequency wiggle vs feature deletion), and a perceptually-weighted metric built from measured thresholds predicts human quality judgments far better than existing boundary metrics - which misrank a meaningful share of comparisons.
why_important: Boundary quality ultimately serves human consumers (editors, clinicians); a psychophysically-grounded metric would reset how boundary progress is scored.
why_possibly_novel: Threshold-measurement-based metric construction for segmentation boundaries is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: 2AFC discrimination study over parameterized boundary distortions, fit threshold model, validate on preference prediction of real model outputs.
main_risk: Perceptual weights may be task-dependent (editing vs measuring); collect per use case.

one_liner: Polygon-vs-pixel ground truth is a hidden treatment: rasterization conventions systematically bias boundary supervision across datasets.
problem: Masks originate as polygons (COCO), brush strokes, or pixel labels, each with different rasterization and corner behavior; models trained across datasets inherit conflicting micro-boundary conventions.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: a classifier can identify a mask's annotation tool from boundary micro-statistics alone with high accuracy (tool fingerprints exist), and cross-dataset boundary-metric gaps shrink measurably after fingerprint-normalizing GT - part of 'domain gap' in boundary quality is tooling, not imagery.
why_important: Identifies an ignored confounder in every cross-dataset boundary comparison and offers a normalization remedy.
why_possibly_novel: Annotation-tool fingerprint forensics on mask boundaries is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Train tool classifier on masks from datasets with known tooling, apply cross-dataset, re-evaluate transfer gaps after harmonizing rasterization.
main_risk: Tool and content are confounded across datasets; validate fingerprints on same-content multi-tool annotations.

one_liner: For small objects, context carries most of the information: measure the interior-vs-context information ratio as a function of object size.
problem: Small objects have few interior pixels; recognition may rest almost entirely on context. The interior/context information balance as a function of size has not been quantified, though it dictates correct architecture and augmentation choices.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: masking object interiors reduces small-object segmentation accuracy by far less than masking equivalent context rings, with the interior contribution rising steeply above ~32px - a measurable crossover implying sub-crossover objects are 'context-defined' and interior-focused methods are wasted on them.
why_important: Explains why small-object performance resists resolution increases in some regimes, and quantifies exactly what supervision small objects need.
why_possibly_novel: Size-conditional information-source decomposition is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Interior/context masking sweeps across object-size bins on COCO/LVIS, plot information-ratio curves per class family.
main_risk: Masking artifacts; use multiple fill strategies and report agreement.

one_liner: GPU-budget-matched showdown: high-resolution crops vs bigger models for small-object segmentation.
problem: Two competing recipes claim small-object gains - spend compute on resolution (crops, tiling) or on capacity (larger backbones). They are never compared at matched total compute, so the field lacks an exchange rate.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: at matched training+inference FLOPs, resolution investment dominates capacity investment for objects below ~2% image area (with a measurable crossover size), and the advantage compounds under domain shift because resolution gains are shift-invariant while capacity gains partially memorize.
why_important: An exchange-rate law between resolution and capacity would guide every deployment with small objects (aerial, medical, defect inspection).
why_possibly_novel: Budget-matched resolution-vs-capacity frontier for dense prediction is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Grid of (resolution, model size) at fixed FLOP budgets on aerial + medical datasets, map iso-compute performance contours vs object size.
main_risk: Conclusions may be architecture-family-specific; replicate across CNN and ViT families.

one_liner: Optimal polygon click budget allocation: where should an annotator spend the next vertex for maximal mask fidelity?
problem: Polygon annotation spends vertices uniformly or by habit, but boundary information density varies enormously along contours (corners vs straight runs); the optimal allocation policy and its savings are unknown.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: curvature-adaptive vertex allocation achieves target boundary fidelity with 30-50% fewer clicks than uniform or annotator-natural allocation (measurable on re-annotation studies), and existing dataset polygons are far from the efficient frontier - quantifying wasted annotation spend at ecosystem scale.
why_important: Annotation budgets are the binding constraint on dataset scale; a proven allocation policy converts directly into more labeled data per dollar.
why_possibly_novel: Information-theoretic vertex-allocation analysis of real datasets is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Compute fidelity-vs-vertex-count curves for optimal (dynamic programming on GT contours) vs actual COCO polygons; run small human study with guided placement.
main_risk: Human motor/attention costs may not follow vertex-count economics; the human study is the decisive leg.

one_liner: Per-class signed boundary bias: models systematically over- or under-segment each class by a constant offset that morphological recalibration removes.
problem: Boundary error is reported as unsigned distance, hiding a possible constant signed bias per class (e.g. 'person' always 2px eroded, 'sky' always dilated) that would be trivially correctable if measured.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: a large fraction of per-class boundary error is a constant signed offset (bias, not variance) stable across images and datasets for a given model - and per-class morphological recalibration (single dilation/erosion parameter fitted on validation) recovers a large share of boundary-metric error at zero architecture cost.
why_important: Free accuracy lying on the table for every deployed model, plus a diagnostic separating systematic from stochastic boundary behavior.
why_possibly_novel: Signed-bias decomposition with recalibration accounting is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Measure per-class signed boundary offsets for 5 public models, fit recalibration on val, report test boundary-metric recovery.
main_risk: Bias may vary with object scale/context, making constant-offset correction too crude - measure the residual structure.

one_liner: Corners are the hardest pixels: boundary error grows superlinearly with local curvature, exposing decoders as low-pass shape filters.
problem: Errors concentrate at high-curvature boundary features (fingertips, leaf tips, corners), consistent with spectral bias, but the error-vs-curvature law and its architecture dependence have not been established.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: boundary displacement error grows superlinearly with local GT curvature, with an architecture-specific cutoff frequency measurable from the error spectrum - CNNs and ViTs show different cutoff signatures, and the cutoff predicts performance on curvature-heavy domains (text, machinery, foliage) better than aggregate metrics.
why_important: A transferable spectral characterization of decoders enables domain-model matching from first principles (measure domain curvature spectrum, pick decoder with adequate cutoff).
why_possibly_novel: Curvature-resolved error laws with spectral cutoffs are UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Bin boundary errors by local curvature across model zoo and datasets, fit error-vs-curvature laws, extract cutoffs, validate domain-matching predictions.
main_risk: Curvature estimation on noisy GT is delicate; use analytically-known synthetic shapes as anchors.

one_liner: Uncertainty glint: tiny objects announce themselves as anomalous uncertainty texture even when the class prediction misses them entirely.
problem: Small objects below the detection threshold often leave no trace in hard predictions, but they may perturb the model's uncertainty/feature maps in a detectable way - a second-channel signal for recall recovery.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: at locations of missed small objects, per-pixel predictive-entropy neighborhoods have statistically distinct texture (localized entropy spikes) relative to matched background, supporting a recall-recovery detector that finds a meaningful fraction of misses at low false-positive cost - the model 'flinches' where it cannot 'see'.
why_important: Missed small objects are the costliest errors in screening applications; harvesting sub-threshold evidence directly attacks the recall frontier.
why_possibly_novel: Uncertainty-texture mining for sub-threshold objects is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: On LVIS/aerial datasets, extract entropy-map patches at missed-object locations vs matched negatives, train shallow detector, report recall-at-FPR added.
main_risk: Entropy spikes also occur at texture boundaries; the discriminator must beat that base rate.

one_liner: Stuff-stuff boundaries are measure-zero fictions: grass-to-sidewalk transitions are physically bands, and the label model should say so.
problem: Between stuff classes (grass/dirt, sand/water) there is often a mixed transition band, not a curve. Datasets draw arbitrary curves through the band, and models are penalized for reasonable placements within it.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: annotator agreement within stuff-stuff transition bands is near chance (band placement is arbitrary), band widths are measurable and class-pair-specific, and introducing band-aware evaluation (no penalty within measured band) changes stuff-class rankings while leaving thing-class rankings intact - showing current stuff boundary scores are substantially noise.
why_important: Stuff classes dominate scene area; noise-driven rankings there corrupt aggregate metrics that guide the field.
why_possibly_novel: Transition-band measurement and band-aware evaluation is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Multi-annotate stuff transitions on ADE/Cityscapes subsets, measure band widths, re-score public models band-aware.
main_risk: Some stuff transitions ARE sharp (curb edges); the method must classify band vs edge cases first.

one_liner: Below the annotation noise floor: SOTA claims on tiny-object benchmarks assert precision the labels cannot support.
problem: For an 8px object, a 1px annotation error swings IoU by tens of points. Benchmarks report tiny-object metrics to decimals without computing the label-noise floor, so some published gains are unfalsifiable.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: propagating measured annotation position noise through IoU for small size bins yields uncertainty intervals wider than most published method-to-method gaps in those bins - a decisive fraction of tiny-object SOTA claims are statistically vacuous, and the community's smallest evaluable object size is derivable per dataset.
why_important: Defines the epistemic limit of small-object benchmarking and prevents wasted effort chasing noise.
why_possibly_novel: Noise-floor-derived minimum-evaluable-size analysis is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Estimate annotation jitter from double-labeled subsets, Monte-Carlo propagate through size-binned metrics, overlay published deltas.
main_risk: Jitter estimates from small double-labeled samples have their own uncertainty; report meta-intervals.

one_liner: Sub-stride phase determines tiny-object visibility: shifting the image by 8 pixels changes which small objects a model finds.
problem: Feature-map stride quantizes where evidence lands; a tiny object's alignment with the stride grid (its phase) may decide detection - implying single-pass evaluation undercounts model capability and phase-TTA recovers it.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: per-object detection outcomes for sub-stride objects flip with input translation at rates far above large-object rates (phase sensitivity), aggregate phase-averaged recall exceeds single-phase recall substantially, and phase sensitivity per architecture is predictable from its stride pyramid - a deterministic, correctable component of small-object failure.
why_important: Distinguishes 'cannot represent' from 'unlucky alignment', with an immediately usable inference fix and a design principle (anti-aliased strides) validated by the phase signature.
why_possibly_novel: Systematic phase-sensitivity accounting for small-object segmentation is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search (shift-variance of CNNs in general is KNOWN).
minimal_experiment: Translate test images over a stride-period grid, measure per-object outcome flip rates by size, evaluate phase-ensembled recall.
main_risk: Border effects from translation; use central-crop evaluation regions.

one_liner: Shadow edges poison boundary supervision: models trained with gradient-aligned boundary rewards learn to follow illumination, not objects.
problem: Many pipelines sharpen boundaries using image gradients (CRF-style refinement, edge-guided training). Shadow edges are strong gradients that do not bound objects; the systematic confusion rate this induces is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: models with gradient-coupled boundary refinement place object boundaries onto shadow edges at measurably higher rates than gradient-free models (a shadow-following bias), and the bias grows with refinement strength - quantifying a hidden cost of a ubiquitous technique and predicting its failure in harsh-light domains (aerial noon imagery, surgical lighting).
why_important: CRF/edge-guidance is folklore-good; measuring its shadow tax would qualify decades of accepted practice with domain-specific guidance.
why_possibly_novel: Shadow-specific failure accounting of gradient-based refinement is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Curate shadow-crossing object boundaries, compare boundary placement of refined vs unrefined variants of the same models, sweep refinement strength.
main_risk: Isolating refinement as the only difference requires careful model surgery; use toggleable refinement implementations.

one_liner: Hairline cracks defeat both training and evaluation: 1-pixel objects need sub-pixel offset-field formulations, not masks.
problem: Infrastructure cracks, cell membranes, and hairline defects are ~1px structures where binary masks cannot even represent the target faithfully, yet the field forces mask formulations onto them.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: representing thin structures as sub-pixel center-line + width fields (continuous offsets) instead of binary masks improves BOTH detection recall and downstream measurement accuracy (crack width estimation) at matched supervision cost, because the continuous formulation matches the object's actual dimensionality - falsifiable by direct formulation comparison.
why_important: Thin-structure measurement is an economically huge application (infrastructure inspection) currently served by a mismatched formulation.
why_possibly_novel: KNOWN: center-line representations exist in vessel literature; the sub-pixel measurement-accuracy comparison against mask formulations at matched supervision is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: On crack datasets with caliper-measured widths, train mask vs offset-field formulations, compare detection and physical-measurement error.
main_risk: Requires physically-measured GT (width calipers); small but real collection effort.

one_liner: Depth-of-field is a per-pixel boundary-sharpness oracle that models ignore: defocused boundaries deserve wide predictions, focused ones sharp.
problem: Within one photo, optical defocus varies boundary sharpness continuously, but models emit uniform-sharpness boundaries everywhere - a mismatch between optics and output that nobody exploits or measures.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: model boundary error correlates strongly with local defocus (measurable via blur estimation), models do NOT modulate their boundary confidence with defocus (uniform sharpness output), and defocus-conditioned evaluation reveals current boundary metrics penalize physically-inevitable uncertainty as if it were model error.
why_important: Separates optical information limits from model limits per pixel, enabling fairer evaluation and defocus-aware outputs for editing applications.
why_possibly_novel: Defocus-conditioned boundary analysis is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Estimate local blur on benchmark images, bin boundary errors by blur level, test whether model confidence tracks blur.
main_risk: Blur estimation errors propagate; use focal-stack captures with known defocus as calibration.

one_liner: Contour-domain error autocorrelation reveals each decoder's effective receptive field along boundaries - a fingerprint measurable without internals.
problem: How far boundary errors correlate ALONG the contour (error wavelength) encodes the decoder's spatial coupling, but boundary evaluation collapses everything to scalars, discarding this diagnostic structure.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: the autocorrelation length of signed boundary error along contours is a stable architecture fingerprint (invariant across datasets, distinct across model families), predicts which post-processing helps (short-wavelength errors respond to smoothing, long-wavelength to re-recognition), and can identify anonymous model families from outputs alone.
why_important: Gives practitioners a black-box diagnostic that prescribes the right fix, and gives forensics a model-attribution tool.
why_possibly_novel: Contour-frequency-domain error analysis is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Compute along-contour error spectra for 8 public models over 3 datasets, test cross-dataset stability and family separability.
main_risk: Contour parameterization ambiguities at junctions; restrict to simple closed contours initially.

one_liner: Upstream JPEG kills small objects before the model ever sees them: pipeline compression bounds recall independent of model quality.
problem: Data pipelines (dashcams, drones, cloud upload) compress images before inference; tiny low-contrast objects may be erased at the compression stage, making model improvements irrelevant - yet compression is absent from benchmark methodology.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: for objects under ~12px, realistic pipeline compression (bitrates of deployed dashcams/drones) removes recoverable evidence for a large fraction of instances (verified by human inspection of decompressed crops), establishing a compression-determined recall ceiling that no model surpasses - and benchmark images, being lightly compressed, systematically overstate deployable recall.
why_important: Redirects small-object investment toward capture/codec policy where the recall is actually lost, with quantitative ceilings per bitrate.
why_possibly_novel: Compression-ceiling accounting for small-object segmentation is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Re-compress benchmarks at deployment bitrates, measure model + human recall ceilings vs original, tabulate evidence destruction per size bin.
main_risk: Codec diversity (H.264/H.265/AV1) requires a matrix, not a single number.

one_liner: Attribute the small-object gap: with oracle localization, is segmentation of small objects actually solved?
problem: Small-object segmentation failure conflates finding (localization) and delineating (mask quality). The conditional performance - mask quality GIVEN correct localization - isolates which stage fails.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: conditioned on oracle boxes, small-object mask quality is close to large-object mask quality (normalized for pixel count), so the small-object problem is >80% a search/detection problem, not a segmentation problem - implying segmentation-architecture work on small objects is largely misdirected.
why_important: Cleanly splits a conflated problem and reallocates effort to the failing stage (search strategies, high-recall proposals).
why_possibly_novel: Stage-conditional gap attribution for small objects is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Evaluate promptable and two-stage models with GT-box prompts across size bins, compare conditional mask quality profiles.
main_risk: Normalizing mask quality across sizes is subtle (IoU size-sensitivity); use boundary-normalized metrics.

one_liner: Decompose boundary uncertainty into normal and tangential components: only normal errors matter, and metrics that mix them misrank methods.
problem: Boundary deviations perpendicular to the contour (position error) change the region; deviations along it (parameterization wiggle) often do not matter - yet distance-based boundary metrics penalize both indiscriminately.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: decomposing boundary error into normal/tangential components shows the tangential component contributes substantial metric variance while being nearly uncorrelated with human quality judgments and downstream task success - normal-only metrics agree better with both, and re-scoring benchmarks with them changes method orderings.
why_important: A geometrically-principled metric correction that removes a systematic noise source from all boundary evaluation.
why_possibly_novel: Normal/tangential decomposition for segmentation evaluation is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Implement decomposed metrics, re-score model zoo, correlate both components with human preferences from a small study.
main_risk: Correspondence between predicted and GT contours is ambiguous at large errors; define robust matching first.

one_liner: Instance merging obeys a crowding law: adjacent-instance merge probability is a universal function of gap-to-size ratio, like human visual crowding.
problem: Dense instances (cells, crowds, grapes) get merged by segmenters. If merge probability follows a universal law in dimensionless gap/size units - analogous to crowding in human peripheral vision (KNOWN: Bouma's law) - dense-scene capability could be predicted and compared principledly.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: merge probability across models and domains collapses onto a single curve in (gap/object-size, contrast) coordinates with model-specific scale factors - a 'machine Bouma law' - enabling dataset-independent dense-scene capability ratings and principled prediction of failure density in novel domains.
why_important: Universal laws compress messy benchmarks into transferable engineering constants; a crowding constant per model would be a durable, comparable capability spec.
why_possibly_novel: Dimensionless-collapse analysis of instance merging is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Measure merge rates on synthetic instance grids (controlled gap/size/contrast) plus cell/crowd datasets, test curve collapse across 5 models.
main_risk: Real-scene occlusion patterns may break the two-parameter description; add occlusion fraction as third axis if needed.

one_liner: Models have a blob prior: error statistics reveal systematic shape simplification toward compact blobs, measurable as a shape-frequency transfer function.
problem: Predictions tend toward smoother, rounder shapes than GT, but 'shape simplification' has never been characterized as a transfer function (which shape frequencies are attenuated how much) that would make the bias precisely correctable and comparable.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: comparing shape-descriptor spectra (elliptic Fourier coefficients) of predictions vs GT yields a stable per-model attenuation curve (the blob-prior transfer function), consistent across datasets, whose inverse partially restores fine shape structure post hoc - shape bias is a measurable filter, not a vague tendency.
why_important: Converts a folklore bias into an engineering object (measurable, invertible, comparable across models) with direct value for shape-critical applications (typography, machining, biology morphometrics).
why_possibly_novel: Transfer-function characterization of segmentation shape bias is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Compute EFD spectra ratios prediction/GT per model, verify cross-dataset stability, test spectral re-inflation on held-out data.
main_risk: Inversion amplifies noise along with signal; regularized inversion needed and honest failure reporting.

one_liner: Photograph printed calibration shapes to get camera-true boundary ground truth with exact sub-pixel geometry - the first zero-annotation boundary benchmark.
problem: All boundary evaluation inherits annotation noise. Printing precisely-known vector shapes, photographing them under controlled conditions, and registering the known geometry yields ground truth with certainty no annotator can provide - yet no such benchmark exists for segmentation.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: a physically-photographed benchmark of exactly-known shapes (varying size, curvature, contrast, blur, texture) will reveal sub-pixel systematic biases of segmentation models (chromatic offsets, contrast-dependent placement, curvature attenuation) that are invisible on annotated data because they are smaller than annotation noise - opening a metrology-grade regime of boundary science.
why_important: Establishes an absolute measurement foundation the entire boundary literature lacks; every sharpness/bias claim becomes precisely testable.
why_possibly_novel: Metrology-style physical-ground-truth benchmarks for segmentation are UNVERIFIED - needs lit search (camera calibration targets are KNOWN but serve geometry, not segmentation evaluation).
minimal_experiment: Print vector shape set, photograph across cameras/lighting/scales, register via fiducials, evaluate model zoo at sub-pixel precision.
main_risk: Printed shapes are unnatural stimuli; complement with textured/embedded variants to test ecological validity.
